text: {"answer":"The passages mostly indicate that raising the minimum wage does not substantially reduce overall employment, though the evidence is contested. A UK meta-regression of 236 elasticities from 16 studies finds no overall practically significant adverse employment effect, and it flags residential home care as a possible genuine exception [5f591435f1d8#0]. A review co-authored by Dube reports that most US minimum wage studies find no job losses or only small disemployment effects [f3df8a818b8c#0], and a study of low-wage jobs finds the overall count essentially unchanged over five years [e0f83db9d354#1]. Some work also reports that the lack of job loss is not explained by labor-labor substitution at the bottom of the distribution [e0f83db9d354#1]. The contradicting side is real but weaker. A Congressional Budget Office estimate of a $15 federal minimum wage projected about 1.4 million fewer jobs [6de9116294ca#3]. A study of federal increases found significant negative effects on employment and income growth for targeted low-skilled workers [ab2ba547baf0#1]. A review of the literature notes that disemployment effects are stronger for the least-skilled groups [39a319a8bc00#2], and an analysis of teen unemployment links wage hikes to higher teen joblessness [59c7d48f7cbf#0]. Overall, small or no aggregate job loss is the better-supported view, but effects on the least-skilled and teens are less settled.","confidence":62,"one_line":"Mostly no significant aggregate job loss from modest hikes, but CBO estimates and studies of least-skilled and teen workers show disemployment risks."}
